variants.title: Run the bounded controller
variants.context: The controller, not the model, owns the request. It classifies risk and difficulty, reserves one deadline and spend envelope, generates evidence, evaluates the state against the stopping rule, and emits exactly one explicit terminal outcome.
variants.prompt: A code migration request arrives and the repository has a fast test suite. Put the controller stages in order.

items.text: Reserve the envelope: wall time, tokens, candidate count, tool calls, and verifier calls.
Generate evidence: sample diverse candidate patches inside the reserved attempt limit.
Evaluate the state: run the tests, then compare evidence and remaining budget with the acceptance rule.
Classify the decision: material impact, reversible, and an objective checker exists.
Stop explicitly: accept the candidate that cleared the predeclared checks and record the stop reason.

variants.hint: Who decides whether another attempt is allowed?
variants.explanation: Classify, reserve, generate, evaluate, stop. A deterministic controller owns the envelope and every run ends in one declared terminal state.

variants.title: Run the bounded controller
variants.context: The controller, not the model, owns the request. It classifies risk and difficulty, reserves one deadline and spend envelope, generates evidence, evaluates the state against the stopping rule, and emits exactly one explicit terminal outcome.
variants.prompt: An eligibility recommendation cannot be checked automatically at request time and cannot be reversed. Put the controller stages in order.

items.text: Generate evidence: retrieve sources and assemble the material a reviewer will need.
Reserve the envelope and mark accountable review as part of the acceptance contract.
Evaluate the state: the evidence floor is met, but no automatic check can accept the answer.
Classify the decision: high impact, not recoverable, and no objective checker is available.
Stop explicitly: escalate to a qualified person with the assembled evidence and context.

variants.hint: More model compute cannot create missing authority.
variants.explanation: When the acceptance rule requires accountability, the terminal state is escalation with evidence, not another sample.

variants.title: Run the bounded controller
variants.context: The controller, not the model, owns the request. It classifies risk and difficulty, reserves one deadline and spend envelope, generates evidence, evaluates the state against the stopping rule, and emits exactly one explicit terminal outcome.
variants.prompt: A hard request runs out of deadline before the evidence floor is reached. Put the controller stages in order, ending with the terminal state.

items.text: Reserve a deadline, a spend ceiling, and a maximum attempt count before the first call.
Stop explicitly: cancel outstanding work and return a bounded failure instead of an under-supported answer.
Classify the request as hard on its measured difficulty slice.
Evaluate the state and find the deadline reached while evidence is still below the floor.
Charge every candidate and tool call against that single envelope as work proceeds.

variants.hint: A deadline without cancellation keeps spending after the user has gone.
variants.explanation: Budget exhaustion is a terminal state with its own handling: cancel outstanding work and return a truthful bounded failure.

variants.title: Design the stop policy
variants.context: A stopping rule is written before traffic arrives. State the acceptance rule, evaluate whether each new attempt adds independent evidence, compare the marginal gain with latency and spend, then emit a terminal state.
variants.prompt: A team is writing the stop policy for a new route before it serves traffic. Put the design steps in order.

items.text: Compare the expected value of another step with its latency, spend, and timeout risk.
State the acceptance rule: required checks, agreement, source quality, review ownership, and residual risk.
Emit a terminal state: accept with evidence, escalate with context, ask for clarification, or fail.
Evaluate each new attempt for whether it adds independent evidence or repeats an existing path.

variants.hint: The acceptance rule is written before the first token, not after the answer looks good.
variants.explanation: A stopping rule is a contract between evidence and action, so it has to exist before the run that has to satisfy it.

variants.title: Design the stop policy
variants.context: A stopping rule is written before traffic arrives. State the acceptance rule, evaluate whether each new attempt adds independent evidence, compare the marginal gain with latency and spend, then emit a terminal state.
variants.prompt: The second candidate arrives and repeats the reasoning of the first, word for word in its key steps. Put the controller's steps in order.

items.text: Compare the marginal gain of a third sample with the latency and spend it would add.
Evaluate the second candidate and find that it repeats an existing path rather than adding evidence.
Emit a terminal state: escalate with context instead of paying for the same reasoning again.
Recall the acceptance rule this slice declared, including what counts as independent support.

variants.hint: Agreement between copies of one path is not new evidence.
variants.explanation: Correlated candidates create false confidence, so the controller stops or seeks independent evidence rather than sampling the same path again.

variants.title: Design the stop policy
variants.context: A stopping rule is written before traffic arrives. State the acceptance rule, evaluate whether each new attempt adds independent evidence, compare the marginal gain with latency and spend, then emit a terminal state.
variants.prompt: An easy slice, one the baseline already answers correctly most of the time, reaches its deterministic check on the first attempt. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Evaluate the first attempt against the deterministic check it must pass.
Compare the value of another attempt with the latency it would add on an easy slice.
State the acceptance rule and the residual risk this low-impact slice may carry.
Emit a terminal state: accept with the recorded evidence and stop spending.

variants.hint: Stopping early is a decision the policy has to allow.
variants.explanation: Overthinking easy requests adds latency without changing the outcome, so the policy needs a direct path that ends as soon as the rule is met.

variants.title: Charge work to one envelope
variants.context: Every candidate, selector pass, tool call, and verification is charged to one request envelope of wall time and spend. Running work in parallel shortens the wall clock but does not remove any of its compute cost.
variants.prompt: A controller holds a 6,000 ms deadline. Each candidate generation costs 1,200 ms and the objective check costs 700 ms, all on the critical path. After two candidates and one check, how many milliseconds of the deadline remain?
variants.hint: Count everything that ran on the critical path, not only the model calls.
variants.explanation: The verifier spends the same deadline as the generator, so both are charged to the one envelope the request owns.

mistakes.feedback: That charges the two candidates only and leaves the verifier out of the deadline.
That counts one candidate instead of the two that ran.

variants.title: Charge work to one envelope
variants.context: Every candidate, selector pass, tool call, and verification is charged to one request envelope of wall time and spend. Running work in parallel shortens the wall clock but does not remove any of its compute cost.
variants.prompt: The same request has a ceiling of 8.0 cost units. A candidate costs 1.5 units and a verification costs 0.4 units. Three candidates and one verification have already been charged. How many further candidates fit inside the ceiling?
variants.hint: A partial candidate produces nothing, so round the leftover budget down.
variants.explanation: Reserve against the ceiling before starting downstream work; only whole candidates that fit the remaining units may be started.

mistakes.feedback: That divides the whole ceiling by the candidate cost and ignores what has already been spent.
That drops the verification charge and rounds the leftover units up rather than down.

variants.title: Charge work to one envelope
variants.context: Every candidate, selector pass, tool call, and verification is charged to one request envelope of wall time and spend. Running work in parallel shortens the wall clock but does not remove any of its compute cost.
variants.prompt: A fan-out route generates four candidates at 1.5 cost units each, runs one selector pass at 0.6 units, and one verification at 0.4 units. What is the total cost charged to the parent request, in cost units?
variants.hint: Selection and verification are part of the route, not free overhead.
variants.explanation: One user request can become many downstream calls, and every one of them is charged to the parent request's envelope.

mistakes.feedback: That charges the four candidates only; the selector and verifier are charged to the same request.
That charges one candidate; running candidates in parallel saves wall time, not compute.

variants.title: Pick the mechanism that adds evidence
variants.context: Extra compute helps only when it produces the evidence that is missing. Deterministic checks fit objectively checkable outputs, plan search fits decomposable problems, retrieval fits external facts, and an easy slice needs a direct path rather than a wider search.
variants.prompt: A refactor must preserve behavior across three dependent modules, and the repository has a fast test suite. The envelope allows several model calls. Which policy spends it best?
options: Sample several candidate patches and select the one the test suite proves behavior preserving.
Let one trajectory reason for twice as long and return whatever patch it settles on.
Escalate to the stronger model tier before any candidate has been tested.
optionFeedback: Diverse candidates plus a deterministic selector turn extra compute into checkable evidence.
A longer single trajectory produces no independent check of the result it reaches.
A stronger tier costs more latency and spend without proving behavior is preserved.
variants.hint: Which mechanism produces something a machine can check?
variants.explanation: Use deterministic verification for outputs with an objective check, and let the checker, not the model, select the candidate.

variants.title: Pick the mechanism that adds evidence
variants.context: Extra compute helps only when it produces the evidence that is missing. Deterministic checks fit objectively checkable outputs, plan search fits decomposable problems, retrieval fits external facts, and an easy slice needs a direct path rather than a wider search.
variants.prompt: A scheduling task splits into steps whose partial assignments can be scored before the plan is complete. Which mechanism fits this shape?
options: Expand, score, and prune intermediate states so weak branches stop early.
Generate twenty complete plans and accept the answer most of them share.
Give one trajectory a much larger reasoning budget and take its final plan.
optionFeedback: Search over plans fits decomposable problems with meaningful partial evaluations.
Agreement among complete plans shows repetition, and no selector distinguishes the good one.
A single longer trajectory never evaluates the alternatives it did not take.
variants.hint: Can the problem be scored before it is finished?
variants.explanation: Match the mechanism to the task shape: stateful search pays off when intermediate states can be evaluated and pruned.

variants.title: Pick the mechanism that adds evidence
variants.context: Extra compute helps only when it produces the evidence that is missing. Deterministic checks fit objectively checkable outputs, plan search fits decomposable problems, retrieval fits external facts, and an easy slice needs a direct path rather than a wider search.
variants.prompt: A support lookup that the baseline answers correctly on 86 percent of comparable requests is routed through a five-candidate policy. p95 latency tripled and measured accuracy did not move. What should the router do?
options: Send this slice to the direct path and keep the wider budget for hard slices.
Keep the policy, because additional candidates cannot make quality worse.
Raise the agreement threshold so the extra candidates carry more weight.
optionFeedback: Route from measured slice difficulty and maintain a direct path for slices the baseline already solves.
Extra candidates cost latency and spend, which is a real cost even when accuracy holds.
A higher threshold on correlated candidates adds delay without adding independent evidence.
variants.hint: What did the extra compute actually buy on this slice?
variants.explanation: Overthinking easy requests is a failure mode: route by measured difficulty so the budget goes where it changes outcomes.

variants.title: Read the signals correctly
variants.context: Difficulty, impact, verifiability, and recoverability are separate routing signals. The evidence signals are not interchangeable either: confidence is a model output, agreement is repetition, a verifier has its own coverage, and approval assigns accountability.
variants.prompt: A router is being designed and the team keeps collapsing four signals into one score. Match each routing signal to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Difficulty
pairs.detail: How often does the baseline policy already solve comparable requests?

pairs.label: Impact
pairs.detail: What happens if this answer is wrong, late, or unavailable?

pairs.label: Verifiability
pairs.detail: Can code, a database, or a source document check the result?

pairs.label: Recoverability
pairs.detail: Can the user cheaply notice the error and reverse it?

variants.hint: Each signal answers a different question about the same request.
variants.explanation: Prompt length and model confidence are weak substitutes for classifying difficulty, impact, verifiability, and recoverability separately.

variants.title: Read the signals correctly
variants.context: Difficulty, impact, verifiability, and recoverability are separate routing signals. The evidence signals are not interchangeable either: confidence is a model output, agreement is repetition, a verifier has its own coverage, and approval assigns accountability.
variants.prompt: An acceptance rule cites four signals as if they were equivalent proof. Match each signal to the limit it carries.

pairs.label: Model confidence
pairs.detail: A model output that may be miscalibrated

pairs.label: Candidate agreement
pairs.detail: Repeated outputs, which is not independent truth

pairs.label: Verifier score
pairs.detail: Trustworthy only within that verifier's coverage and independence

pairs.label: Human approval
pairs.detail: Assigns accountability but still needs evidence and review time

variants.hint: Ask what each signal can prove on its own.
variants.explanation: These signals are not interchangeable, so an acceptance rule has to name which one it requires and why that one is sufficient.

variants.title: Read the signals correctly
variants.context: Difficulty, impact, verifiability, and recoverability are separate routing signals. The evidence signals are not interchangeable either: confidence is a model output, agreement is repetition, a verifier has its own coverage, and approval assigns accountability.
variants.prompt: A review of four production incidents names four failure modes. Match each one to the correction the design calls for.

pairs.label: Correlated candidates
pairs.detail: Add meaningful diversity or independent evidence instead of more identical samples

pairs.label: Verifier collusion
pairs.detail: Add deterministic checks, source grounding, or a separately designed reviewer

pairs.label: Best-of-many without a selector
pairs.detail: Measure selected-answer quality rather than oracle coverage

pairs.label: Deadline without cancellation
pairs.detail: Use cooperative cancellation so background work stops spending

variants.hint: Each fix restores something the failure removed.
variants.explanation: Naming the failure mode picks the fix: independence for correlation, a separate checker for collusion, selection quality for coverage claims, and cancellation for abandoned work.
